relations.evidence: To drop an unnamed primary index, use the `DROP PRIMARY INDEX` statement. To drop a named primary index, use the `DROP INDEX` statement.

relations.subject: sdk:query-index-manager
relations.reused_or_minted_predicate: reused - same predicate shape as the statement-choice relation above, applied here to SDK-vs-SQL++ rather than statement-vs-statement
relations.evidence: The SDK calls only enable you to drop indexes in the default collection and default scope within a bucket. A SQL++ statement enables you to drop indexes in _any_ collection and scope within a bucket.

relations.subject: sdk:query-index-manager
relations.evidence: The Java SDK does not provide a call for dropping a named primary index. To drop a named primary index, use a SQL++ query.

relations.subject: n1ql:drop-index
relations.evidence: For more information and examples, see [DROP PRIMARY INDEX](../n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/dropprimaryindex.md) and [DROP INDEX](../n1ql/n1ql-language-reference/dropindex.md).

notable_absence.finding: No privilege table is shown on this guide page for either DROP INDEX or DROP PRIMARY INDEX, though both statement-reference pages carry one (Write/Query Index privileges by cluster access credential type). Consistent with the same absence noted on create-index.json - the guide layer never restates access control.

cross_component_finding: This page restates the same alternate-syntax fact ('Specify the index name...or...specify the keyspace and index name using dotted notation') independently for both primary and secondary index dropping, and states a real replica-cascade behavior not present in the DROP INDEX statement-reference extraction seen so far: 'Dropping an index that has replicas will also drop all of the replica indexes too.' This ties n1ql:drop-index to the indexes:index-replication concept behaviourally, though no separate relation was minted for it since it reads as a single incidental fact rather than a recurring pattern.
